points.title: 是 — “to be”
points.short: links two nouns: A is B
points.explain: 是 links two nouns and means “A is B”. Put it between the subject and the noun that describes it. Pitfall: do not use 是 before adjectives — say 我很忙, not 我是忙.

points.title: 的 — possession
points.explain: 的 works like English “'s”: 我的书 is “my book”. The owner comes first, then 的, then the thing. With close family and friends, 的 is often dropped: 我妈妈.

points.title: 吗 — yes/no questions
points.short: turns a statement into yes/no question
points.explain: Add 吗 to the end of a statement to make a yes/no question. The word order does not change. Pitfall: don't use 吗 together with question words like 什么 or 谁.

points.title: 什么 / 谁 — what, who
points.explain: 什么 (what) and 谁 (who) stay in the same place as the answer would. 你叫什么名字？ — 我叫…. Do not add 吗 to these questions.

examples.en: What do you want to eat?

points.title: 不 — “not”
points.explain: 不 goes before a verb or adjective to make it negative. It is used for the present, the future and habits. Before a fourth tone, 不 is read bú (不是, 不去).

examples.en: I'm not going to school tomorrow.

points.title: 很 + adjective
points.short: describes with an adjective, no 是
points.explain: Adjectives can be the predicate directly, without 是. Usually 很 is put before the adjective; it often just links and is not a strong “very”. Pitfall: 我是忙 is wrong — say 我很忙.

points.title: 这 / 那 — this, that
points.explain: 这 means “this” (near) and 那 means “that” (far). Before a noun, add a measure word: 这个人, 那本书. Plural forms are 这些 and 那些.

points.title: 哪儿 / 哪 — where, which
points.pattern: Subject + 在 + 哪儿？ / 哪 + MW + Noun
points.explain: 哪儿 (or 哪里) asks “where”: 你在哪儿？ 哪 + measure word asks “which”: 哪个. Note the tone: 哪 (nǎ, which) vs 那 (nà, that).

points.title: 在 — “to be at”
points.explain: 在 as a verb means “to be (located) at”. Put the place right after it. Pitfall: don't use 是 for location — say 他在家, not 他是家.

examples.en: Your book is on the table.
The teacher is not at school.

points.title: 有 — “to have”
points.explain: 有 means “to have”. Put the thing owned after it. Pitfall: the negative is 没有, never 不有.

points.title: 没有 — “not have”
points.explain: To say “don't have”, use 没有 (or just 没). 不 cannot be used with 有. 没有 is also a short answer meaning “no, I don't”.

examples.en: I don't have an older sister.

points.title: Numbers 一 to 一百
points.pattern: 十 + digit / digit + 十 / 一百
points.explain: Chinese numbers are built logically: 十一 is 11, 二十 is 20, 二十五 is 25, 一百 is 100. Read phone numbers digit by digit; 一 is often read yāo in phone numbers.

examples.en: This book costs a hundred kuai.

points.title: Measure words 个 / 本 / 杯
points.explain: In Chinese you cannot put a number directly before a noun; a measure word goes in between. 个 is the most common one; 本 is for books and 杯 for cups. Also use it after 这/那: 这个.

examples.en: Please give me a glass of water.
There are five people in his family.

points.title: 两 vs 二 — “two”
points.short: 两 counts two things; 二 counts
points.explain: Use 两 before a measure word to say “two of something”: 两个人. Use 二 when counting, in numbers like 十二, and for “second” (第二). Pitfall: 二个人 is wrong.

examples.en: I want two cups of tea.

points.title: 几 / 多少 — how many
points.pattern: 几 + MW + Noun？ / 多少 (+ Noun)？
points.short: asks how many or how much
points.explain: 几 asks about small numbers (usually under 10) and needs a measure word: 几个. 多少 is for any number, often larger, and the measure word can be left out. Use 多少钱 for prices.

examples.en: How many people are in your family?
How many children do you have?
How many students does your school have?

points.title: Age with 岁
points.explain: To say age, put the number and 岁 after the person, usually with no verb: 我二十岁. Ask a child 你几岁？ and an adult 你多大？ The negative needs 不是: 他不是十岁.

points.title: Dates: 年 月 号 星期
points.pattern: 年 + 月 + 号 + 星期
points.explain: Dates go from big to small: year, month, day, weekday. Months are number + 月 (三月 = March); weekdays are 星期 + number, but Sunday is 星期天. Use 几 to ask: 今天几号？

points.title: Clock time: 点 / 分 / 半
points.pattern: Number + 点 (+ Number + 分 / 半)
points.explain: Hours use 点 and minutes use 分: 八点十分 is 8:10. 半 means half past: 三点半 is 3:30. Two o'clock is 两点, not 二点.

points.title: Time words go before the verb
points.explain: Time words like 今天, 明天, 晚上 or 八点 go before the verb, either after the subject or at the start of the sentence. Pitfall: never put them at the end as in English (我去北京明天 is wrong).

examples.en: He watches TV in the evening.

points.title: 在 + place + verb
points.explain: To say where you do something, put 在 + place before the verb. Pitfall: the place does not go at the end like in English (我学习在家 is wrong).

points.title: Place words 上 / 里 / 边
points.pattern: Noun + 上 / 里 / 前边…
points.short: noun + 上/里: on, in, near
points.explain: To say “on the table” or “in the room”, put the position word after the noun: 桌子上, 房间里. 前边, 后边, 旁边 etc. also work alone or after a noun. Pitfall: the order is the opposite of English.

examples.en: The book is on the table.
The store is next to the school.
There are trees in front of my home.

points.title: 有 — “there is”
points.short: says what exists in a place
points.explain: Start with a place, then 有, then the thing: 桌子上有一本书 “there is a book on the table”. Compare 在, which starts with the thing: 书在桌子上. The negative is 没有.

examples.en: There is a book on the table.
Is there anyone in the room?
There is a store next to the school.
There is no water in the cup.

points.title: 也 — “also”
points.explain: 也 means “also, too”. It always goes after the subject and before the verb or adjective. Pitfall: never put 也 at the end of the sentence like English “too”.

points.title: 都 — “all, both”
points.explain: 都 means “all” or “both”. It refers to the people or things before it and goes before the verb. With 也, the order is 也都. 都不 means “none”.

examples.en: My dad and mom are both doctors.

points.title: 呢 — “and you?”
points.explain: Put 呢 after a noun to ask the same question about it: 我很好，你呢？ It also asks where someone or something is: 我的手机呢？

examples.en: I'm a student; what about you?

points.title: 吧 — suggestions
points.explain: 吧 at the end of a sentence makes a suggestion or soft request: 我们走吧 “let's go”. It can also ask for confirmation: 你是老师吧？ “you're a teacher, right?”

examples.en: Why don't you take a rest.

points.title: Verb 不 Verb questions
points.explain: Another way to ask a yes/no question is to say the verb or adjective twice with 不 in between: 你去不去？ Pitfall: don't add 吗 to this kind of question.

examples.en: Are you a teacher or not?

points.title: 还是 — “or” in questions
points.explain: 还是 means “or” in questions where the listener chooses: 你喝茶还是喝水？ Don't add 吗 to the end. It is for questions only.

examples.en: Do you drink tea or water?
Is he a teacher or a student?
Are you going today or tomorrow?
Is this one bigger or that one?

points.title: 和 — “and” (nouns)
points.explain: 和 links nouns or pronouns: 我和你 “you and me”. Pitfall: 和 does not join two sentences or verbs — don't use it like English “and then”.

examples.en: Dad and Mom are both at home.

examples.text: 我有一个哥哥和一个妹妹。
examples.en: I have an older brother and a younger sister.

points.title: 太…了 — “too / so”
points.explain: 太 + adjective + 了 shows a strong feeling: “too…” or “so…!” 太好了！ means “Great!” In the negative, 不太 means “not very” and has no 了.

points.title: 想 / 要 — want to
points.explain: 想 + verb means “would like to”; 要 + verb is stronger, “want to / am going to”. 要 can also be followed by a noun: 我要一杯茶. The negative is usually 不想.

examples.en: I'd like to go to China.
Where would you like to go?

points.title: 会 — can (learned skill)
points.explain: 会 means “can” for skills you learned, like speaking a language or driving. Pitfall: for being allowed or physically able, use 能 instead.

points.title: 能 — can (able, allowed)
points.explain: 能 means “can” in the sense of being able or allowed. 我能进来吗？ asks permission. Compare 会, which is for learned skills.

examples.en: Can I make a call here?

points.title: 了 — completed action
points.explain: 了 after a verb shows that an action has happened or been completed. The negative uses 没 and drops 了: 我没去. Pitfall: 了 is not simply a past tense — don't use it for past habits or with 是.

points.title: 没 — didn't
points.explain: 没 (or 没有) before a verb means the action did not happen. Use it instead of 不 for the past. Pitfall: don't keep 了 after the verb in a 没 sentence.

points.title: 正在…呢 — in progress
points.explain: 正在 (or 在, or 正) before a verb shows an action is happening right now, like English “-ing”. 呢 is often added at the end. Pitfall: 是 and 有 cannot take 正在.

points.title: 请 — please / invite
points.pattern: 请 + Verb / 请 + Person + Verb
points.explain: 请 at the start of a request means “please”: 请坐. With a person after it, it means “invite / ask someone to do”: 我请你吃饭 “I'll treat you to a meal”.

examples.en: I'll treat you to a meal.

points.title: 别 — don't
points.explain: 别 before a verb tells someone “don't”. It is like 不要. Add 了 for “stop doing”: 别说了.

points.title: Two verbs in a row
points.explain: Chinese can put two verb phrases one after another: first going somewhere, then the purpose. 我去商店买东西 means “I go to the store to buy things”. No word for “to” is needed.

examples.en: I go to the store to buy things.
He came to China to study Chinese.
We go to a restaurant to eat.
She goes to Beijing by plane.

points.title: 来 / 去 — come & go
points.short: direction: toward or away from speaker
points.explain: 来 means movement toward the speaker and 去 means away from the speaker. They can follow other verbs: 进来 “come in”, 回去 “go back”, 出去 “go out”.

points.title: Result complements 见 / 到 / 完
points.explain: A second word after a verb shows the result of the action: 看 “look” → 看见 “see”, 找 “look for” → 找到 “find”. The negative uses 没: 我没看见.

points.title: Verb + 一下儿 / VV — “a bit”
points.explain: Add 一下儿 after a verb, or say the verb twice, to mean “do it a little” or “give it a try”. It makes requests sound softer: 请等一下儿.

examples.en: Let me look at your book.

points.title: 跟…一起 — together with
points.pattern: A 跟 / 和 B 一起 + Verb
points.explain: 跟 (or 和) + person + 一起 + verb means “do something together with someone”. The whole phrase goes before the verb.

examples.en: He watches TV with his mom.

points.title: 从 — “from”
points.explain: 从 means “from” for a place or a time. 从…到… means “from… to…”. The 从 phrase goes before the verb.

examples.en: He came out of the house.
It's far from school to my home.

points.title: 比 — comparisons
points.short: compares: A is more … than B
points.explain: A 比 B + adjective means “A is more … than B”. Pitfall: don't put 很 before the adjective (他比我很高 is wrong). Add 一点儿 or 多了 after it for “a bit / much”.

examples.en: This one is more expensive than that one.
My brother is two years older than me.

points.title: 最 — the most
points.explain: 最 before an adjective or verb means “the most”. 最好 means “best”, and 最喜欢 means “like best”.

examples.en: He is the tallest in our class.

points.title: 是…的 — when / how it happened
points.pattern: Subject + 是 + Detail + Verb + 的
points.explain: Use 是…的 to talk about the details of something that already happened: when, where or how. Put the detail after 是 and 的 at the end. 是 can be dropped, but 的 cannot.

points.title: 给 — to / for
points.pattern: 给 + Person + Verb / Verb + 给 + Person
points.explain: As a verb, 给 means “to give”: 给我一本书. Before another verb it means “to / for someone”: 给妈妈打电话 “call Mom”.

examples.en: He gives me a piece of bread.
He bought a book for me.

points.title: 一点儿 — a little
points.pattern: Verb + 一点儿 / Adj + 一点儿
points.explain: 一点儿 means “a little”. After a verb it is a small amount: 喝一点儿水. After an adjective it means “a bit more”: 快一点儿. Pitfall: don't put it before an adjective to mean “a bit” (一点儿贵 is wrong).

examples.en: I can speak a little Chinese.
This one is a bit bigger.

points.title: 怎么 — how
points.explain: 怎么 + verb asks “how” to do something: 怎么去？ “how do I get there?” 怎么了？ asks “what's wrong?”

examples.en: How do you read this character?
How do I get to the airport?
How do you come to school?
